clue.text: Golf course offering a couple of slices?

blocks.note: first meaning: a Kent town whose Royal St George's links hosts the Open
second meaning: a snack of filling between two pieces of bread

explanation.surface: A golfer complains that the links invites hooks and slices.
explanation.walkthrough: Slices look like bad golf shots, but here they are slices of bread. Sandwich is a town in Kent with a famous championship course.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kent town names its championship links, and the snack is filling held between two bread pieces.

clue.text: Bitter when the bill requires driving licence, for example, and one gets caught

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
a driving licence is an example of identification, ID
the Roman numeral for one
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A customer is sour when asked for photo identification before paying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Requires' is padding in the surface that also leads on to the identification; 'and' joins the last pieces on.
explanation.definitionFit: Acidic food or remarks are sharp and sour in taste or tone, a direct synonym for bitter.

clue.text: Rugby player's interpretation of soft and loud

indicators.note: an interpretation is a fresh reading of something, so the letters are read in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
f, forte, is the musical marking for loud

explanation.surface: A rugby player reads the music direction marking loud and soft passages.
explanation.walkthrough: Soft and loud look like musical p and f, but only loud is abbreviated; soft stays as a word.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby union the stand-off, or fly-half, is the back who links the scrum-half with the three-quarters.

indicators.note: without ends means lacking both its first and last letters, so they are cut away

blocks.note: a stick-and-ball team game

explanation.surface: A match that never seems to end is finally finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Over and the answer are synonyms as prepositions, both meaning on the far side of, as in a bridge over or across a river.

indicators.note: something unorthodox departs from the usual form, so the letters leave their usual order

blocks.note: the name and the article, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A dissenter is given a mock-regal title like a Viking chief: Eric the Unorthodox.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a nickname in the style of Eric the Red; 'Unorthodox' also fits the definition, an apt touch.
explanation.definitionFit: A heretic holds beliefs contrary to established religious doctrine, so is a rebel within a faith.

clue.text: Explorer returns to business and leaves from the Americas

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the name is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: John Cabot, the Venetian navigator who sailed to North America for England
Co is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: A voyager comes back to trade, then sails away from the New World.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb of departure, but it is the noun: the dried leaves of a plant native to the Americas.
explanation.definitionFit: The crop is the cured leaves of a New World plant, first brought to Europe from the Americas.

clue.text: One perseveres with hearts, when spades 9

indicators.note: 9 points to the answer at 9 down, meaning put at the front, so one piece leads the other

blocks.note: S is the card-suit abbreviation for spades
ticker is slang for the heart

explanation.surface: A card player keeps going with hearts until spades become trumps.
explanation.walkthrough: The 9 is a cross-reference: read it as the answer to 9 down, PLACED FIRST. Card suits mislead; only spades is an abbreviation, and hearts means the organ.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sticks at a task, refusing to give up, is informally called a sticker.

clue.text: Given the title and script failed, I abandoned cast

indicators.note: abandoned means left behind, so this letter is dropped from the mix
to cast is to throw, and the remaining letters are thrown into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the letter to be dropped

explanation.surface: An actor quits the cast after the script flops, despite the play winning a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: One I from SCRIPT FAILED goes, leaving eleven letters to rearrange. 'Cast' looks like the actors; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor placed first in a contest is declared the champion and so given the title.

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
someone asleep is in bed, so the boy goes inside this word

explanation.surface: A clever lad, or perhaps one dozing off?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags an indirect step: 'asleep' gives no letters directly but tells you the boy is in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bladed has a cutting edge, so is sharp in the physical sense of a knife or tool.

clue.text: Car going south from Leeds to Belfast?

blocks.note: the M1 motorway runs south from Leeds to London, with 1 written as I
Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland, NI

explanation.surface: A driver plans a trip south out of Leeds and on to Belfast.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is England's main north-south motorway, ending at Leeds; the digit 1 doubles as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mini is the small British car first made in 1959 and still sold today.

blocks.note: the cuckoo is a bird, here in the possessive
a pit is a hollow, a sheltered resting place like a nest

explanation.surface: An insect's froth is found lining a bird's nest.
explanation.walkthrough: Cuckoos famously build no nest of their own, a joke behind the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The frothy blobs on plants in spring are made by froghopper nymphs, and are commonly called by this name.

clue.text: Forsaken the Lord God? Then we finish!

annotation.answer: THE END OF THE WORLD IS NIGH

definitions.text: Forsaken the Lord God? Then we finish!

indicators.note: forsaken means abandoned and left in ruins, so the following words lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A preacher warns that if we abandon God, humanity is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: the doom-laden warning of a placard-carrying prophet, made from twenty-two letters of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Apocalyptic street preachers proclaim this slogan, warning that a godless people faces imminent final judgment.

indicators.note: negotiated suggests worked around and reworked, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A treaty about shipping terms is hammered out bit by bit.
explanation.definitionFit: Navigators record distance travelled east as eastings, a term from sailing and map grids.

clue.text: Morning sickness is good in Victoria's house

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: Queen Victoria was the last monarch of the House of Hanover
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A royal pregnancy brings morning sickness to the palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Morning sickness' suggests pregnancy, but it is the sick feeling after a night's drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangover is the headache and nausea felt the morning after heavy drinking, a jokey reading of the phrase.

clue.text: Figure to spell misery without a 'y'

indicators.note: without a 'y' tells the solver to drop that one letter from the word

blocks.note: a hex is a witch's spell
agony is extreme misery

explanation.surface: Trying to work out how to spell misery without its final y.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell' looks like writing letters out, but it is a magic spell.
explanation.definitionFit: A geometrical figure is a plane shape, and a six-sided polygon is one such shape.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone whose mind is confused
setter's reading: an intellectual's head is pictured as an egg, so the contents could be scrambled like eggs

explanation.walkthrough: Scrambled brains suggests confusion, the opposite of the answer, an intellectual.
explanation.definitionFit: A highbrow intellectual is called this informally, from the image of a large bald dome of a head.

indicators.note: an introduction is an opening, so without it the first letter is lost

blocks.note: someone who bets is a better, a gambler

explanation.surface: A dull writer is improved by dropping his opening.
explanation.walkthrough: Three routes: a walker, the thriller writer Eric Ambler, and 'better' as one who bets. 'Pedestrian' looks like an adjective, dull, but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone strolling on foot is an ambler, a pedestrian; Eric Ambler wrote spy thrillers.

clue.text: Robin Hood was one who won't get Dick Whittington's job

definitions.text: who won't get Dick Whittington's job

blocks.note: first meaning: a bowman

blocks.clueFragment: who won't get Dick Whittington's job
blocks.note: second meaning: Jeffrey, the novelist and peer who withdrew as candidate for Mayor of London in 1999

explanation.walkthrough: Dick Whittington was Lord Mayor of London; Jeffrey Archer, the Tory candidate for the new mayoralty, quit the race in a perjury scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: The outlaw of Sherwood was a famous bowman, and the topical politician shares that surname.

clue.text: Cor blimey mate, noise and abuse is terrible, but I love it so in song!

annotation.answer: MAYBE IT'S BECAUSE I'M A LONDONER

definitions.text: I love it so in song

indicators.note: terrible means in an awful state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.clueFragment: Cor blimey mate, noise and abuse
blocks.note: taken as written, every letter

explanation.surface: A Cockney admits the racket and insults are awful, yet still loves the old town.
explanation.walkthrough: Cor blimey is a Cockney exclamation of surprise; the song is Hubert Gregg's music-hall-style anthem to London, which goes on 'that I love London so'.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's next line declares deep affection for the city, so it is the song of that sentiment.

indicators.note: what is worn goes around the wearer, so one piece sits outside the other

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
loth is a spelling of loath, reluctant

explanation.surface: Someone reluctant to put on their Sunday best for church.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress someone is to put clothes on them, a straight synonym as verbs.

indicators.note: deposited means placed or laid down inside something

blocks.note: to feign is to fake
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A stranger passes off counterfeit gold at the bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Something foreign is strange or alien to a person, not known from experience.

blocks.note: first meaning: widespread, held by most people
second meaning: a senior army rank

explanation.walkthrough: 'A commanding position' sounds like high ground; it is a top military rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A general view is one commonly accepted, and a general is a high-ranking officer who commands armies.
